To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have measured the masses of the individual components of the μ Orionis quadruple-star system with relative precision of 5%, 15%, and 1.5%, that we have measured their orbital coplanarities with relative precision of about 6%, that we have established that the system is a quadruple-star, and that we have measured its distance and luminosities.

we have used the PHASES instrument to measure the positions of the four components of the quadruple-star μ Ori with a median precision of 20 micro- arcseconds and have determined the masses, distances, and mutual inclinations of the two pairs of stars in this system.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the new PHASES data have enabled us to determine the masses, luminosities, and relative inclinations of the components in these complex systems, and to establish the coplanarity of the orbits.

, with the PHASES data and analysis, we have been able to determine the orientation of the long-period orbit of μ Orionis to be 140 degrees and the orientation of the A–Ab subsystem to be 136 degrees.

the new PHASES measurements of the complex μ Ori system are consistent with the predictions of recent theoretical models of hierarchical systems and the masses of the system components are consistent with the masses of other similar systems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PHASES is capable of measuring the mutual inclination between inner and outer orbital planes to precisions that are comparable to the predicted peak of the relative inclinations distribution.
differential astrometry with precisions on the order of 1–10 μas can be used to constrain the mutual inclinations of multiple star systems.

the PHASES data have enabled a detailed characterization of the complex orbital dynamics of this quadruple system and have provided new insights into the orbital dynamics of hierarchical quadruple-star systems.
